CONSEQUENTIAL NEWS
- Alaska Senate suit thrown out (Nov 1; NYT, Politico, AP). The Justice Department sued Oct 22-23, at Trump's direction and before any votes were counted, to head off certification of a possible win by Democrat Mary Peltola over Republican Sen. Dan Sullivan. The theory: a second candidate also named Dan Sullivan is on the ballot, and the NYT reported Peltola's campaign staff helped recruit him as a spoiler (her campaign denies it). DOJ amended the suit Oct 29 to seek decertifying the result if Sullivan loses narrowly, and asked to set aside ballots for the second Sullivan; Alaska's attorney general called that "disturbing and impossible" on privacy grounds. Judge Sharon Gleason dismissed it, saying there is no workable plan for handling two Dan Sullivans; DOJ says it will appeal, and its criminal inquiry (about 40 subpoenas) and the House Oversight probe by Rep. James Comer continue. Sullivan says he will accept the results. | Consequence: hurts the Maximalists (the faction that runs the enforcement agencies, DOJ and FBI included) on the midterms. This was their main tool for contesting a Peltola win, and the criminal probes remain the path left. Their score on the midterms was cut from +1 to 0 (documented).
- Ninth Circuit rejects DOJ's California ballot appeal (Oct 30, AP via WDBO; the newsletters ran it Nov 1). DOJ is running a criminal noncitizen-voting probe in Los Angeles County (subpoenas to three registrar employees, a grand jury date of Nov 4) and asked a federal judge to set aside about 20,000 mail ballots. Judge Carter refused and appointed a special master. A 2-1 Ninth Circuit panel dismissed DOJ's emergency appeal Oct 26, then on Oct 30 rejected its main appeal, finding "no feasible way" to separate the ballots. DOJ says it will go to the Supreme Court. | Consequence: a second court loss for the Maximalists on contesting the midterm count, so the stored ruling was raised to a "shift" (documented).
- Axios: "tough" Trump-Netanyahu call about Iran (Nov 2; reported, one outlet). The US and Israel have held back from striking Iran again until after the Nov 3 midterms; the WSJ reported Oct 28 that Gulf states were told to prepare for a short, intense campaign after Nov 3. Axios's Barak Ravid reports Netanyahu pressed Trump on the call to strike right after the election, while Trump said he is "not in much of a hurry" and prefers to let talks play out, with talks and combat preparation running together. | Consequence: weakens the Primacist Hawks (Rubio, Hegseth, Miller and others who want a harder line on Iran) and helps the Vance Lane, which favors the talks track. It also cuts against our stored expectation of a quick campaign after Nov 3; provisional, because it rests on one outlet.
- Iran says the "ball is in the US court" (Nov 2; Al Jazeera, CBS; Iran's own claim). Qatar presented Iran a seven-day draft deal Oct 25; Iran rejected Qatar's ideas Oct 28, saying "no concessions on the nuclear issue"; Qatari mediators then returned to Tehran with a revised proposal and an Iranian answer was due by the end of last week. Iran now says its answer has gone to Washington through Qatar, with terms unpublished. Oil fell on the news (Semafor); Iran's leader separately ordered a "geographically unrestricted" response to any new US attack. | Consequence: closes our pending item on Iran's reply; the choice between a deal and strikes now rests with Trump, with the Treasury squeeze camp and the Operation (his political team) preferring to wait. Only Iran's characterization; not independently confirmed.
- Rep. Haley Stevens endorses Republican Mike Rogers (Nov 1; Axios, NYT, AP). Stevens (D-Mich.) lost the Michigan Democratic Senate primary to Abdul El-Sayed, who faces Rogers in Tuesday's general election. Two days before it she endorsed Rogers; staff resigned, Schumer called it "a despicable betrayal," some House Democrats want her removed from the caucus, and Trump said he would "love to have" her in the Republican Party. AOC had called her privately to try to stop it. El-Sayed raised $1.2M within hours. | Consequence: helps the Party Machine (the RNC and Senate campaign committees) in a seat both parties are fighting over (my reading; provisional).
- Trump and Canadian PM Mark Carney speak by phone (Nov 2; Politico Playbook, Reuters). Canada is under 50% tariffs, imposed under Section 338, that apply even to USMCA goods and took effect Oct 30; an importer suit challenging them was filed Oct 20, and Carney said Oct 30 Canada would wait out this administration if needed. After the call Trump said the sides are "very close" and described a "concept" of a new trade deal with Keystone XL on the agenda; Carney called it a good conversation and said they will meet in coming weeks. | Consequence: a possible opening in the tariff fight, but statements only, with no terms (reported).
- Russia-Ukraine local truce at Oleshky ends (Nov 1; Al Jazeera, AP). A six-day ceasefire in Russian-occupied Oleshky (Kherson region), mediated by Melania Trump with Pope Leo XIV rather than by the US government, let civilians evacuate. It ended Nov 1 with no reported violations and no extension, and both sides' air-raid alert apps were hacked afterward (Ukraine's sent false nuclear and chemical warnings). | Consequence: no change in any faction's position; the stored Russia pending line was updated (reported).
